title: Rama's calm
hook: everyone in the palace wants someone to blame, and Rama won't

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm, with his mother, until her grief turned to blessing. Were you the steady one for someone? Today, the question of blame, and the end of a week. Day five hundred twenty-five.

Who did this? In Ayodhya today, the question has three answers ready: Kaikeyi, Manthara, the king. Knowing who's responsible matters; it's how a wrong gets named and mended. But a hunt for blame can become its own fire, and burn longer than the thing that started it. Lakshmana is already reaching for the names. Rama is the one person with every right to say them out loud. And he refuses.
screen: `WHO DID THIS?` → `BLAME CAN BECOME ITS OWN FIRE.` → `RAMA REFUSES THE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana is still burning, and Rama speaks to him directly. Put away the things gathered for the coronation, he says, and help me get ready to go. Then he talks about Kaikeyi, and it's surprising. Don't blame her, he says. She has never treated me differently from her own son. If she has suddenly asked for this, cruel as it is, something larger than her is at work. The word Rama uses is daiva, what comes from the gods, what we'd call fate or destiny. No one, he says, can fight what is given in this way. Happiness and sorrow, gain and loss, birth and death, they come, and nobody fully knows why. It would be easy to hear this as giving up. But look at what it does in the story. It takes the hatred out of the room. Rama isn't saying Kaikeyi did nothing. He's saying he won't make her the enemy, because she was once a mother to him and may be again. Lakshmana will argue the other side soon, and Valmiki will let him. Today, notice just this: Rama uses the idea to protect someone who has hurt him. And look back at the whole week. A maid's plan. An old promise claimed. A king's night of pleading. A morning when a father could only say his son's name. And three days of Rama's calm: so be it to Kaikeyi, steadiness for his mother, and now, no blame for anyone.
screen: `PUT AWAY THE CORONATION THINGS.` · `DON'T BLAME KAIKEYI.` · `DAIVA: WHAT THE GODS GIVE.` · `TAKING THE HATRED OUT OF THE ROOM.` · then, large: `A WEEK: A PLAN, A PROMISE, A CALM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of someone you've been blaming for something, large or small. Picture their face. Without deciding they were right, try for a moment to see them the way Rama saw Kaikeyi: as someone who was once kind to you, and might be again. Breathe in. Breathe out, and loosen your grip on their name. You can pick it back up later if you need to. The bell holds the time.
Rama's calm, toward blame. He tells Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi, calling what happened daiva, something larger than any one person.
Your line: Rama's calm. Today, when something goes wrong, fix what you can before you go looking for whose fault it is. Day five hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Sanskrit texts name two forces, daiva, fate or what the gods give, and purushakara, human effort; in the Ramayana the two sides are spoken by two brothers, Rama here and Lakshmana soon after.

fork.setup: you're Rama. your brother wants to name and punish the person who did this. what do you say?
options: Kaikeyi did this; she'll answer for it.
don't blame her; this is daiva.
fork.reveal: Rama refuses to make Kaikeyi the enemy: she treated him like a son, and what happened is larger than her.

original.note: Sanskrit daiva: what comes from the devas, the gods; fate, destiny. Rama's word for what has happened.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama says it's fate because he's given up.
what it means: he uses daiva to refuse to make Kaikeyi an enemy.
what a scholar hears: the pairing of daiva and purushakara, fate and human effort, appears in other Sanskrit texts too, and here Valmiki gives each side to a brother.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 22 (Rama to Lakshmana on daiva; not blaming Kaikeyi)
